senses: A traditional spearthrower, consisting of a stick with a hooked end, used by First Nations Australians.
A monetary unit used in a number of central and northern European countries, known locally as daalder (Netherlands), daler (Scandinavia), Taler, Thaler (Germany), etc.
The currency of Baden from 1829 to 1837, valued at 100 Kreuzer.
ety: Borrowed from German Thaler, an abbreviation of Joachimsthaler, after Sankt Joachimsthal, the German city in which some of the earliest thalers were minted in 1518. Doublet of dollar and tolar.

senses: The science that deals with climates, and investigates their phenomena and causes.
The excessive concentration of population and development in a single centre, to the detriment of other areas.
A person who grasps
A tool used for grasping
Grandmother.
One who approves or gives approval.
The process of removing a cause from an inferior court to the supreme court.
ety: From Latin advocātiō. Doublet of advowson

senses: To separate a region in a way that turns it into an exclave.
A layer of fat, along the back of a pig, used as a cut of meat or to make lard
A fish, the menhaden.
The root of such a plant, or an extract of these roots.
ety: Borrowed from Hokkien 人參 /人参 (jîn-sim, “ginseng”). Doublet of ninzin.

senses: One of the thin strips into which sugar beets are cut as part of the sugar-making process.
An open-sided dwelling with a thatched roof made of dried palm leaves.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish palapa, from Tagalog palapa (“midrib of a coconut frond”), from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *palaqpaq.
examples: At the average home price, you can find a two- or even three-bedroom house with a pool and palapa.

senses: A male witch; warlock.
A human who has undergone a controlled mutation so that he can kill monsters as a professional mercenary in Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher series.
ety: From witch + -er, a male equivalent of witch using the -er suffix as masculine, as in widower vs. widow, a calque of Polish wiedźmin. Possibly influenced by witchery. The Polish word was coined in 1986 by author Andrzej Sapkowski as a male equivalent of wiedźma (“witch”) for his The Witcher book series and media franchise. The English calque witcher was popularized by the series' English translation.

senses: The act of deactivating something, such as a bomb or alarm.
A pastry made from multiple thin layers of dough rolled up and filled with fruit, etc.
A vertical hole in sea ice through which downward jet-like, buoyancy-driven drainage of flood water is thought to occur.
Infected with mange; mangy.
The night office of the Christian liturgy of the Hours, such as is performed in monasteries.
A portion of the psalter used during nocturns.
ety: From Middle English nocturne, borrowed from Medieval Latin nocturna, noun use of the feminine form of Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal, of the night”), derived from nox (“night”).

senses: The hamate bone.
ety: From Latin hamus (“hook”) + -ate (adjective forming suffix); the noun is a back-formation from hamate bone, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

senses: The act or process of increasing pressure within a space.
The digit zero.
A cycle rickshaw
A large cured meat sausage of Italian origin, served in slices.
ety: From Italian salami, plural of salame (“salami”), from sale (“salt”), from Latin sal.

senses: A traditional Spanish unit of length, equivalent to about 1.67 m.
ety: From Spanish estado (“Spanish fathom, state, status”), from Latin stātus (“standing, state, status”). Doublet of state, status, estate, and stade.

senses: Able to be dimmed: able to have illumination decreased in brightness without blowing out or degrading the service life of the LED or light bulb.
examples: The store is having a sale on dimmable chandeliers.

senses: Mesua ferrea (Ceylon ironwood).
ety: Borrowed from Assamese নাহৰ (nahor), ultimately from Sanskrit नागकेसर (nāgakesara).

senses: Having a richly ornamented harness.
Dressed in richly ornamented finery.
examples: Preceded by the richly caparisoned guards, care had been taken to give them the appearance of an escort necessary to dignity—but not to security.
Nevertheless, a good Turkish meal was enjoyed in the merry company of Customs men and divers gaily-caparisoned officials.

senses: A portrait which depicts two side-by-side subjects with relative proximity.
ety: Borrowed from Latin iugātus (“yoked together in pairs”), perfect passive participle of iugō (“to yoke”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

senses: Situated in front, or outside the margins, of a glacier or ice sheet (and formed from its meltwaters).
A person's precedent or example.
ety: Borrowed from Swahili nyayo (“footsteps, footprints”), from Proto-Bantu [Term?].
examples: Chapos or no chapos, this was a good time to follow my father's nyayo and leave these innovative ladies of Kabete to their poetic cookery.

senses: An overlarge page that is folded into a book or magazine.
A bed that folds out from a closed position.
Having macropores, i.e. pores of a relatively large size (e.g. greater than 50 nanometres).
A subject or theme.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θέμᾰ (thémă). Doublet of theme.
examples: Eco has his own image for this method-spiral repetition: every new exploration elevates the solutions to a higher level by expanding the thema's cognitive context.

senses: Either of two grape varieties grown in Tuscany and Romagna.
Any of several red wines made from these grapes.
Characteristic of mushrooms.
Resembling a mushroom.
Flavoured with mushrooms.
examples: Dried mushrooms are really mushroomier than the canned and very simple to use; they are used a great deal in Chinese and Italian cooking.
It grew steadily colder and presently a mushroomy sort of smell came up from the darkness.

senses: A federal law enforcement officer, usually belonging to the United States government.
ety: Back-formation from the plural, from Mexican Spanish federales, from federal.

senses: A widely cultivated Italian grape variety of high acidity, used in the production of white wine and brandy.
A variety of dry white wine made from this grape.
A railway employee who inspects and maintains the permanent way of a railway installation.
examples: When a passenger or freight train is snowbound, any train crew or passengers must first be rescued and taken to the nearest station. This task is usually done by local trackmen.
Drones and helicopters have been in common use by Network Rail for some time, and are a far cry from the days when all inspections were carried out by trackmen reaching remote sites on foot.

senses: The act of marginalizing.
To make parallel (to each other).
To treat as if parallel; to draw parallels between.
examples: Care must be taken lest the machine parallelize the fibers.
They erroneously parallelized the symptoms of the two diseases.
